top_authentic_signals.name: Live Web Fact-Checking (OSINT)
top_authentic_signals.summary: The research agent found credible reporting that corroborates the depicted event or scene.
top_authentic_signals.what_found: The video clip is known as the "Gimbal" video, one of three Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) videos officially released by the Pentagon. It was recorded on January 21, 2015, by a U.S. Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet pilot from the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group. The footage first gained public attention in December 2017 after being published by The New York Times. The Pentagon formally declassified and released the video in April 2020, confirming its authenticity as genuine military footage depicting unidentified aerial phenomena. While the footage is real, the nature of the object itself remains officially unidentified, with some analyses suggesting the apparent rotation could be a camera artifact.
top_authentic_signals.why_it_matters: Corroborated public reporting supports the underlying event or statement. It still does not prove the file is untouched, so the media-specific detectors remain important.
top_authentic_signals.caveat: OSINT is strongest for public figures, viral claims, and news events. Generic private video clips may have no searchable provenance.

top_ai_signals.name: Spectral Artifacts
top_ai_signals.summary: The Six-Lens model scored this image 79.6% AI and 20.4% authentic, a extremely high-confidence finding toward synthetic generation.
top_ai_signals.what_found: All six spectral lenses, covering visual texture (ConvNeXt), frequency grids (FFT), sensor noise simulation (SRM), color-space fingerprints (YCbCr), spatial reconstruction (SPAI), and robustness testing, collectively scored this image 79.6% AI. At this level, the majority of lenses independently flagged patterns like periodic frequency grids and noise distributions inconsistent with any known camera sensor profile.
top_ai_signals.why_it_matters: This model looks for patterns invisible to the human eye, buried in the pixel-level math of the image. A 79.6% score means the statistical fingerprint aligns significantly more with AI generation than camera physics, and these frequency-domain traces are very hard to remove without visibly degrading the image.
top_ai_signals.caveat: Heavy JPEG compression, aggressive resizing, or strong image filters can partially destroy the frequency-domain signals this model depends on, potentially softening a confident AI detection into an inconclusive result. Conversely, very new or unusual AI generators not present in training data may produce lower-than-expected scores.
